passages.t: A second Passover for those who missed the first
passages.happening:
In the first month of the second year, God tells Moses that Israel is to keep the Passover ‘at its appointed time’ (verse 2). They do so, ‘at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month’ (verse 5).

But some men cannot take part. They have touched a dead body and are unclean. They come to Moses and ask, ‘why should we be excluded from presenting the LORD’s offering with the other Israelites at the appointed time?’ (verse 7). Moses answers, “Wait here until I find out what the LORD commands concerning you” (verse 8).

God gives a new ruling. Anyone who is unclean because of a dead body, or far from home, may keep the Passover one month later, ‘at twilight on the fourteenth day of the second month’ (verse 11), with all its rules. But a person who is clean and at home and simply does not keep it ‘must be cut off from his people’ (verse 13). And a foreigner living among Israel may keep it too: “You are to apply the same statute to both the foreigner and the native of the land” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Like chapter 7, this chapter reaches back before the census that opens the book. It is the first anniversary of the night Israel left Egypt. Before the people leave Sinai, they remember how they came to be free.

Passover was a family meal of lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs, eaten at twilight in memory of the night the LORD struck Egypt's firstborn and passed over the houses of Israel that were marked with blood (Exodus 12). Taking part required a person to be ritually clean, and touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days. In a world where families washed and buried their own dead, someone would often be in that state through no fault of their own.

So the men's question is a fair one, and the story treats it that way. They do not want to be let off. They want to be let in. Moses does not guess at an answer. He waits to hear from God. Numbers has several stories of this kind, in which a case the law has not covered is brought to Moses and a new ruling follows. They show Israel's law as living instruction from a God who is present, and not as a closed book.

God's answer makes a second appointed time for those who missed the first. Centuries later King Hezekiah used this provision and held the Passover ‘in the second month’ (2 Chronicles 30:2). Jewish tradition still marks the date as Pesach Sheni, the Second Passover.

The warning in verse 13 is aimed carefully. The men who were unclean through no fault of their own are given another chance. The warning is for the one who is able and does not care.

Then comes the foreigner. The Hebrew word is ger, a person from elsewhere who lived among Israel without land or family there. In the ancient world a people's religion usually came with birth and nation. Here the festival at the center of Israel's identity is open to outsiders who choose to join, under the one law that applies to everyone.

This is the only Passover the five books of Moses record Israel keeping in the wilderness. The next one mentioned is at Gilgal, after the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 5:10).
passages.later:
The rule that none of the lamb's bones may be broken (verse 12) is quoted by John at the cross. When the soldiers did not break the legs of Jesus, John writes, “Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken’” (John 19:36).

Paul says it outright: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

And he tells believers who were not born into Israel, “Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians 2:19).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that a person who neglects the Passover will be ‘cut off from his people’?

The phrase appears often in the laws of Leviticus and Numbers, and its meaning is debated. One view takes it as a death penalty carried out by the community. Another, argued by Jacob Milgrom among others, holds that it is a punishment God himself carries out, such as an early death or the ending of a family line; in some passages God says, ‘I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people’ (Leviticus 20:3). A third view takes it as being put out of the covenant community. Many interpreters think the phrase could cover more than one of these.

What is clear here is the contrast. A person kept away by circumstances is given a second date. The warning falls on contempt, on the one who could come and will not. It was a law for Israel under the covenant of Sinai, and it is not a threat held over anyone who has missed a church service or a communion.
passages.asks: The men who were shut out asked why they should miss the feast, and God made room for them. Ask who is missing from your church's table because of circumstances no one has thought about: illness, work, distance, grief. And ask whether you yourself are kept away by something real, or have simply stopped bothering.

passages.happening:
“On the day that the tabernacle, the Tent of the Testimony, was set up, the cloud covered it and appeared like fire above the tabernacle from evening until morning” (verse 15).

The cloud governed every move. “Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the Tent, the Israelites would set out, and wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp” (verse 17). Sometimes it stayed for many days, sometimes only overnight. “Whether the cloud lingered for two days, a month, or longer, the Israelites camped and did not set out as long as the cloud remained over the tabernacle; but when it was lifted, they would set out” (verse 22).

“They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The first half of the chapter looked back to Egypt. This half looks ahead to the road.

The cloud was already known from Exodus. It had led Israel out of Egypt as a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and it had filled the tabernacle when the tent was finished. Numbers describes it again now because the march is about to begin, and the cloud will decide every stage of it.

The passage is built on repetition. The Hebrew word for cloud comes eleven times in nine verses. The phrase ‘at the LORD’s command’ comes seven times. The verbs for setting out and camping alternate again and again. A reader is meant to feel what it was like. No one in the camp knew how long a stop would last. It might be one night. It might be a month. The people could not plan the road. They could only watch the tent.

That is a hard way to travel, and the passage does not pretend otherwise. Staying could be as hard as going. Verse 19 notes that even when the cloud lingered for many days, the Israelites ‘kept the LORD’s charge and did not set out’. Waiting is counted here as obedience.

One rule governed all of it. Israel moved when God moved. The chapter tells the reader how the following was meant to work. The next chapters will tell how it went.
passages.later:
Exodus first describes the cloud: “And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night” (Exodus 13:21).

Nehemiah, praying centuries later, saw the cloud as a sign of mercy to a people who had not deserved it: ‘You in Your great compassion did not forsake them in the wilderness. By day the pillar of cloud never turned away from guiding them on their path’ (Nehemiah 9:19).

At the transfiguration of Jesus a cloud covered the mountain, and “a voice came from the cloud, saying, ‘This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!’” (Luke 9:35). Israel followed the cloud. The disciples are told to listen to the Son.
passages.asks: Israel could not know whether a stop would last a night or a month. Ask where you are being made to wait with no date given, and whether you have counted the waiting as wasted time. And ask what it would look like to keep God's charge where you are, until the cloud lifts.
